subject: Context length & concurrency -> GPU pool sizing for Nimble Health

Subject: Context length & concurrency -> GPU pool sizing for Nimble Health

Hi Emily — great talking earlier. Per our call you asked for a concrete sizing recommendation and an example commit structure so your procurement team can budget. Below is the workload profile you shared and a conservative sizing approach so we can iterate: 

Workload summary (from Nimble QA):
- Peak concurrent requests: 180 simultaneous sessions (50–200 range; 95th percentile ~150)
- Average incoming prompt length: 600 tokens (clinic notes + user message)
- Average generated response length: 300 tokens
- QPS observed during weekday peaks: ~90–120 req/s (spiky; 30s bursts)
- Model mix: 60% base Llama2-13B-style variant, 40% 70B-family for clinical summarization
- Caching eligible: ~18% of requests are identical system prompts (templates)

Basic throughput math (conservative):
- Avg tokens per request = 600 + 300 = 900 tokens
- At 120 req/s -> 108,000 tokens/s total

Approx GPU throughput assumptions (typical, varies by kernel/quantization):
- H100 (70B quantized fp16/4-bit): ~30k tokens/s per GPU for mixed-length traffic
- A100-80GB (13B optimized): ~40k tokens/s per GPU for the 13B path (shorter memory overhead)

Naive pool mapping (no caching, no batching gains):
- To cover 108k tokens/s with 70B equivalents: need ~4 H100s (4 * 30k = 120k tokens/s) if everything routed to 70B.
- Given model mix, better to split: 2 H100 for 70B (2*30k=60k) + 2 A100 for 13B (2*40k=80k) -> combined capacity 140k tokens/s (buffer and burst headroom).

Additional operational notes / asks from us:
- Can you share a 1-hour peak sample trace (we requested nimble_throughput_samples.csv) so we can baseline real latency percentiles?
- Do you require 99th-token-latency SLOs at the request level or is P50/P95 sufficient to start?

Initial recommendation: 12-month reserved commit that covers base pool of 2x H100 + 2x A100 with a 25% burst bucket (consumption-based) for ~30% of peak bursts. We can present tiered discounts for 12 vs 24 months.

I will follow up with a price sketch and a runbook for fallback (smaller model routing) and autoscaling boundaries. If that looks reasonable I can loop in finance/procurement for a draft term sheet.

Best,
Soojin
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference

- Our procurement team needs a 99th-percentile end-to-end latency SLO target for the clinical summarization endpoint: <= 750ms, otherwise we won't be able to certify for production. Is that achievable with the proposed split?

Emily — looping in pricing to give you a concrete sketch so procurement can run numbers. High level options (all $ are illustrative list prices):

Option A — 12-month reserved pool (recommended starter)
- Base pool: 2x H100 + 2x A100 dedicated (always-on)
- Burst bucket: equivalent of 1x H100 for 20% of monthly hours (consumption-based)
- Monthly committed spend: $85,000
- Effective unit discount vs on-demand: ~42%

Option B — 24-month reserved pool (best price)
- Same pool, larger burst allowance, plus 5% additional discount
- Monthly committed spend: $78,000

Breakouts and assumptions:
- Pricing includes runtime optimizations (continuous batching, KV caching) but excludes premium observability add-on unless requested.
- We can bake in a 2-week PoC (no charge against commit) to run your sample trace and validate 99th latency for the summarization model. That PoC will produce p50/p95/p99 numbers and a recommended autoscale policy.
- If you need a strict 99th < 750ms SLO we recommend adding the burst bucket or a dedicated hot-path (routing that uses pre-warmed KV caches + shorter-context model variants) for the summarization calls.

Subject: Operational plan & refined sizing after trace review

Emily — I reviewed the sample logs you uploaded and ran it through our internal profiler. Key findings and a refined, operational recommendation below: 

Profiler highlights (1-hour peak window):
- Median tokens/request: 820
- Median response tokens: 320
- Observed cache hit rate: 20% for templated prompts (matches your note)
- Burst periods show short spikes up to 200 req/s for ~45s

Effective numbers after caching/batching gains:
- Adjusted avg tokens/request ~ (0.8*1140 + 0.2*1140*0.0) = ~912 tokens (roughly 20% effective reduction across hits and batching)
- Adjusted sustained tokens/s at 120 req/s -> ~109,440 tokens/s

Refined pool mapping (operational):
- Recommended always-on: 3x A100 (to cover 13B traffic and provide cheaper per-token economics) + 2x H100 (for heavy 70B summarization bursts). This mix favors larger count of smaller GPUs to increase effective concurrency. Estimated sustained capacity: 3*A100(3*40k=120k) + 2*H100(2*30k=60k) = 180k tokens/s raw. With caching/batching headroom we have good buffer for spikes and p99 targets.
- Autoscale: Add 1 H100 on warm standby for fast burst up to 250 req/s; fallback policy: if queue grows > 150ms for token generation, route non-critical summarization to optimized 70B-quantised variant (approx -20% quality delta).

Latency considerations:
- With pre-warmed KV cache + continuous batching and the above mix, our PoC results typically show p99 token latency reductions sufficient to hit <= 700–750ms on this token profile. PoC required to lock p99 number for your exact prompts.

Commit recommendation and pricing impact:
- Targeted 12-month commit that guarantees the always-on 3 A100 + 2 H100 capacity. Include a burst credit pool to cover ~15–25% monthly burst hours.
- If procurement wants lower commit spend, a hybrid 2 A100 + 2 H100 always-on + larger burst pool is an alternative with higher run-rate but lower committed capital.

I'll prepare a runbook for the PoC (scripts, test tokens, expected metrics) and the autoscale knobs so your SREs can validate.

—Marissa
Principal Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
